docs.title: Controlled Flight
docs.text:
argon:controlled_flight is a Palladium flight type with momentum, banking and a body that leans into its direction of travel. It is opt-in: palladium:flight and argon:forced_flight are untouched.

Only the movement feel is new. Flying is still toggled, landed and started the way it is for palladium:flight, and the permitted speed still comes from speed and sprint_speed. That means argon:flight_speed, the flight speed dial and flight slowness all keep working, and the acceleration settings only decide how quickly the player reaches that speed.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
Use it as the flight_type of a palladium:flight ability:

{
    "type": "argon:controlled_flight",
    "profile": "natural",
    "speed": 1.5,
    "sprint_speed": {
        "type": "argon:flight_speed",
        "ability": "fsang:dc/kryptonian/absolute#kryptonian_absolute_flight_speed_adjuster",
        "base": 1.5
    },
    "propelled_sound": "palladium:player.flight.propelled"
}

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
A profile sets the default for every setting below, and any setting can still be given on its own.

Profile Feel controlled Balanced. Smooth acceleration, moderate momentum, settles into a hover. The default. propelled Heavier momentum and slower corrections. Sinks while no direction is held. natural Quick to turn and stop, no gravity. For flight without propulsion. gliding Keeps its heading, gravity always pulls and fades as speed rises, and height and speed trade for each other (see Gliding).

docs.title: Movement
docs.text:
Property What it does flight_acceleration Fraction of the gap to top speed closed per tick when speeding up. flight_deceleration Fraction closed per tick when slowing while a direction is held. Also bleeds speed during sharp reversals. flight_response_curve 1 is constant. Above 1 starts slower and pushes harder near top speed. momentum_retention How much turning is held back at speed. 0 turns as sharply at speed as when slow. turn_responsiveness Degrees the heading can turn per tick at low speed. air_braking_strength Fraction of speed lost per tick when no direction is held. gravity_influence Pull of gravity while no direction is held (always for gliding). hover_stabilization Extra speed removed per tick when almost stopped. hover_velocity_threshold Speed under which hover stabilization starts (it applies up to three times this).

Speed never rises above the permitted top speed because of turning: changes of direction rotate the velocity, and speed only moves toward the target. Speed above it, such as from Charged Takeoff, decays at flight_deceleration.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
Property What it does enable_body_rotation Leans the whole rendered body, with armor, layers and cape, into the direction of travel. lean_start_speed, lean_full_speed Fractions of top speed where the lean starts and where the body is fully aligned. orientation_responsiveness How fast the body follows the direction of travel. enable_flight_banking, max_bank_angle Roll into turns, up to this angle. bank_responsiveness, bank_recovery_speed How fast the bank builds and returns to level. bank_speed_influence How much the bank scales with speed.

The lean is a pitch about the body's own right axis, and nothing else. The body keeps facing the way it normally does, then tips forward or back by the angle of the direction of travel measured in that frame (0 is upright, 90 is horizontal and facing forward, 180 is head down), eased in with speed. The angle is kept continuous, so it carries on past vertical through a loop without flipping, and the body is never turned about any other axis to get there. Bank and barrel roll are then added as a roll about the body's own forward axis (the chest axis when upright, the head axis when leaning), so rolls always spin around the body whichever way it is pointing.

The orientation is a world orientation. While gravity is turning, the model is not carried by the gravity animation: the animated turn is taken out and the final orientation put in, so the body stays where it is in the world while the camera swings. It uses the entity's own look yaw frame and never changes gravity or the hitbox.

The animation handler also fills Palladium's flight Molang queries: palladium.flight_roll is the bank, and palladium.flight_pitch is the forward lean in degrees (negative when leaning back). An animation should not rotate the body bone itself any more, but can use flight_pitch to counter-rotate the head, as the Absolute animation does.

docs.title: Camera
docs.text:
Property What it does camera_roll_mode none, partial (default) or full: how much of the bank the camera rolls by. camera_bank_multiplier The share of the bank used in partial mode. enable_speed_fov, speed_fov_multiplier Widen the field of view with flight speed. Off by default. enable_third_person_framing, third_person_framing_offset Frame the body in third person, with the character at or a little below the middle of the screen. On by default, offset 0.25.

First person is not attached to the body: only the camera bank applies.

In third person the camera frames the body while flying (enable_third_person_framing, on by default). Normally the camera aims at the eyes, so when the body leans or the eye height drops while sprint-flying the character slides off the middle of the screen. The camera now aims at the middle of the body, plus third_person_framing_offset blocks (0.25 by default, which sits the character a little below the middle), eased in and out with the start and end of flight. It follows the player's own up direction, so it works while gravity is turned.

docs.title: Barrel roll
docs.text:
Off by default. With enable_barrel_roll, double-tapping left or right while flying rolls the body once around the direction of travel. There is no new key. The roll is a visual rotation shared with other players, and it pushes the player a little to the side.

Property What it does enable_barrel_roll Turns the double-tap on. barrel_roll_duration Ticks the roll takes (14). barrel_roll_lateral_strength A sideways push as a fraction of top speed (0.3). Forward speed is kept. barrel_roll_cooldown Ticks before another roll (30). barrel_roll_camera_influence How much of the roll the camera follows. 0 keeps the view steady (default), 1 rolls with the body. barrel_roll_min_speed Fraction of top speed needed to start a roll (0.2).

The roll is a model rotation added to the bank, so it follows the same axis as banking and never changes gravity.

docs.title: Collisions
docs.text:
Off by default. With enable_flight_collision, hitting a block or flying into an entity at speed hurts.

Property What it does enable_flight_collision Turns collisions on. flight_impact_speed The impact speed in blocks per tick below which nothing happens (0.45). flight_block_collision_damage Multiplier on block impact damage, worked out from the speed of the impact the way elytra damage is. flight_entity_collision_damage Multiplier on the damage to a flown-into entity. flight_entity_knockback How hard that entity is pushed away. flight_collision_stop Whether an impact stops the player's speed.

The flying client spots the impact from the speed it lost against the block, or the speed it closed on an entity. The server checks that the player is flying with this type, caps the reported speed to about 2.5 times the top speed, applies a short cooldown and works out the damage itself. Blocks use the vanilla fly-into-wall damage and entities take a player attack. Minecraft already sweeps a moving player against block shapes, so fast flight does not pass through walls.

docs.title: Gravity following
docs.text:
Off by default. With enable_gravity_following, gravity follows the direction the player is flying and looking, the way it follows a surface for Wall Crawling, so loops and vertical flight have no pitch limit. It uses Argon's directional gravity (see GRAVITY.md): while flying, the flight adds its own gravity source and the camera and model turn with it.

Property What it does enable_gravity_following Turns it on. gravity_wrap_pitch How far up or down the player has to look, in degrees (30 to 80), before gravity turns. Default 55. gravity_turn_ticks How many ticks the camera and model take to turn. Default 8.

Flying is always aimed by the look direction: the forward key goes where the player is looking, whatever way gravity is turned, unlike Wall Crawling where movement follows the surface.

Once the player looks past gravity_wrap_pitch while pushing forward or moving at least a tenth of top speed, gravity turns 90 degrees about their right side: looking up makes the direction they are facing the new gravity, looking down makes the opposite. After a turn the view sits well inside the new horizon, so turns do not repeat, and keeping on round a loop turns gravity down, forward, up, back and down again. Looking back the other way undoes the last turn, so gravity updates as you fly with no key to press. Nothing turns during the first half second of flight, and merely hovering and looking around never turns it. Each turn keeps the view direction, converts the speed and keeps the player's eye where it is, so the view does not jump and the body swings around the head. Setting gravity_turn_ticks to 0 makes the turn instant.

Gravity only has the six axis directions, so with a heading that is not along an axis the turn uses the nearest one. A turn is skipped if the rotated hitbox would not fit.

Gravity goes back to normal, with the same animated turn, when flight ends. The flight source has a lower priority than Wall Crawling's, and the server removes it if the player is no longer flying with this type.

While gravity is bent, speed, input and view angles are all in the player's own frame, as the gravity framework does for everything else. The look direction the game reports is the world one, so the flight turns it into the player's frame before using it. The ground check for landing looks along the player's own down, and other players' lean is worked out in their own frame.

docs.title: Landing
docs.text:
Controlled flight lands by itself when the player is dropping towards the ground, the way palladium:flight does, but the touchdown is now controlled. Landing starts when the player is dropping more than they are travelling sideways, within a few blocks of a surface (along their own down when gravity is turned), and not faster than landing_speed_threshold.

Property What it does enable_superhero_landing Turns the automatic landing on (default). landing_speed_threshold The downward speed in blocks per tick up to which a landing is controlled. Default 1. landing_recovery_duration Ticks on the ground before flight stops. Moving cancels it early. Default 15. landing_damage_reduction How much of a hard landing's damage is prevented (0 to 1). Default 0.5.

During a landing the descent is slowed in proportion to how far the surface is, down to a soft touchdown, sideways speed bleeds off and the body stands upright. The flight phase is 5 while landing (and 4 while descending), so an animation controller can use palladium.flight_phase() for a landing pose.

A controlled landing deals no damage. Diving faster than the threshold does not brake, and touching the ground then is a hard landing: the flying client reports the speed it hit at, the server caps it and deals fall damage, reduced by landing_damage_reduction. It is ordinary fall damage, so Palladium's fall protection abilities still reduce it, and nothing makes the flight immune.

docs.title: Diving
docs.text:
Off by default. With enable_diving, looking steeply down while pushing forward is a dive. There is no key: it follows the look direction.

Property What it does enable_diving Turns diving on. dive_pitch How far down the player has to look, in degrees (30 to 85). A dive builds up from here and is full at 85. Default 45. dive_acceleration_multiplier The top speed of a full dive as a multiple of the normal top speed (1 to 4). Default 1.6. dive_speed_retention How much of the extra dive speed carries on afterwards. 0 loses it at the normal deceleration, 1 at dive_momentum_decay. Default 0.8. dive_momentum_decay The fraction of the extra speed lost each tick at full retention. Default 0.015. dive_pullout_responsiveness How much easier it is to turn while above top speed, so pulling out does not need a huge circle (1 to 4). Default 1.8.

The permitted speed never changes: it still comes from speed, sprint_speed and the speed level. A dive only lets the player go faster than that for a while, up to the dive speed, and the extra always fades, so it can't build without limit. The body already follows the direction of travel, so a dive shows as head down with no extra setting.

docs.title: Gliding
docs.text: For the gliding profile, speed and height trade for each other: glide_energy_exchange (0 to 0.3, default 0.05) adds speed when the player drops and takes it away when they climb, capped at top speed (or the dive speed when diving is on). glide_lift_speed (0.05 to 1, default 0.6) is the fraction of top speed at which gravity is fully cancelled; slower than that the player sinks, so a glider that stops pushing slowly drops.

docs.title: Animation states
docs.text:
The handler works out a state for every flying player on each client, so animation controllers can pose each one from the same Molang queries:

Query Value argon.flight_state() 0 none, 1 hover, 2 accelerating, 3 cruising, 4 turning, 5 diving, 6 braking, 7 rolling, 8 landing argon.flight_dive() 0 to 1, how deep into a dive argon.flight_rolling() 1 while a barrel roll is happening argon.flight_roll_progress() 0 to 1 through a barrel roll

These sit alongside Palladium's own queries: palladium.flight_phase(), flight_speed_forward, flight_speed_sideways, flight_yaw_delta, flight_roll (the bank), flight_pitch (the lean) and flight_propulsion_scale. Nothing needs animations: the body leans, banks and rolls without any.

docs.title: Directional Gravity
docs.text: title: Directional Gravity menu_title: Directional Gravity blurb: A gravity framework: pull a player toward any of six directions and everything follows.

docs.title: Directional Gravity
docs.text: Argon can pull a player toward any of the six directions instead of down. Everything follows the new gravity: walking, standing, jumping, falling, the hitbox, the eyes, where the player looks, the camera and the drawn model. Wall Crawling uses it to make the surface under the player their floor, and the /argon gravity command lets you try it by hand.

docs.title: Directions
docs.text:
down is normal gravity. Every other direction turns the player so that direction is their floor.

Gravity Floor down The ground, as normal up The ceiling north, south, east, west The wall on that side

Gravity also has a strength, a multiplier from 0 to 10 on how hard it pulls. 1 is normal.

docs.title: What follows the gravity
docs.text:
• Movement and collision. Walking, sprinting, jumping, friction, swimming and elytra steering all behave as they do on a floor. Landing on a surface wins over sliding along it, and stepping up a block steps along the new up.
  • Hitbox. The upright box is turned about the feet. A player who cannot fit lying along a wall drops to the crouch and then crawl pose automatically.
  • Eyes and aiming. The eyes, the view direction, block interaction and aiming all use the new up, so what you point at is what you hit.
  • Falling. Fall distance and fall damage count along the new down, and step sounds follow the new floor.
  • Camera. The camera turns with the gravity, blended over a short time. With rotate_camera off in Wall Crawling, the camera keeps the world's up while the body and physics still turn.
  • Model. The whole model, with its armor, held items and layers, turns about the feet, and other players see the correct orientation.

When gravity changes, the view is recomputed so the player keeps looking at the same point. Aim does not swing; only the roll of the camera changes. The body stays where it is and turns around the edge it was touching, so turning toward a wall you were touching puts your feet on the wall.

docs.title: How the gravity is chosen
docs.text:
Several things can try to bend gravity at once, so each one is a source with a priority.

  • Direction. The source with the highest priority that has a direction wins. Equal priorities go to the most recent one.
  • Strength. The strengths of all sources are multiplied together and limited to 0 to 10. Priority does not matter for strength.
  • Expiry. A source can end after a set time. When it does, the next best source takes over. With no sources left, gravity is normal.
  • Staying after relogging. Only a source marked persistent is saved with the player. Everything else is dropped when the player leaves, and all temporary sources are cleared on death.
  • Suspended. Spectators, passengers and the dying have their gravity put aside, so nobody ends up sideways in a boat or stuck after death.

Surface-walking abilities such as Wall Crawling sit at a lower priority than temporary effects, and commands sit highest.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Needs permission level 2. Each command takes an optional player list and defaults to you.

/argon gravity get [targets]
/argon gravity set <up|down|north|south|east|west> [targets]
/argon gravity reset [targets]
/argon gravity strength <0-10> [targets]
/argon gravity sources [targets]

sources lists what is currently bending gravity, which helps when two abilities disagree.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Players only.
  • Other movement abilities (flight, Charged Takeoff, web swinging, grappling and dashing) move the player in world terms and misbehave while gravity is bent by a command. Run /argon gravity reset before using them. Wall Crawling lets go of the surface by itself when one of them starts.
  • Checks for a block in the eyes (drowning, the in-wall overlay) and the player's name tag still use the upright player, and water under the eyes while lying on a wall is not handled.
  • The name tag, the shadow and the hitbox outline are drawn in the upright frame.
  • Argon cape physics stays upright, and custom player animations are drawn inside the turned frame without being aware of it.

docs.title: Path Vision
docs.text: argon:path_vision shows the holder where nearby entities and projectiles are going. The path is drawn ahead of the target with a Palladium trail. Everything is drawn on the holder's own client and nobody else sees it. The ability only reads existing movement data: it never changes an entity's movement, AI or collision, and never changes a projectile's flight.

docs.title: Adding it to a power
docs.text:
Add it like any other ability. With no other settings it uses the defaults below and Argon's two built in trails.

"path_vision": {
    "type": "argon:path_vision",
    "detection_radius": 24.0,
    "max_targets": 16,
    "entity_trail": "argon:path_vision_entity",
    "projectile_trail": "argon:path_vision_projectile",
    "show_time_to_impact": true,
    "track": ["hostile", "projectiles", "minecraft:villager"],
    "ignore": ["#minecraft:undead"],
    "properties": {
        "icon": "minecraft:ender_eye"
    }
}

It follows Palladium's normal activation: it runs while the ability is unlocked and enabled, so a toggle, a key bind or any enabling condition works. Turning it off, or losing the power, removes every path at once and stops all work on the server and the client.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
General and filtering

Property Default Meaning detection_radius 24.0 Blocks around the holder that are searched. Only loaded entities are ever looked at; no chunk is loaded for a prediction. max_targets 16 Most targets shown at once. target_priority closest Which targets are kept when there are more than max_targets: closest (by distance), hostile_first (hostile mobs before everything else) or projectiles_first. Within a group the closest come first. A "current combat target first" mode does not exist because clients are not told who the holder last attacked. path_update_interval 2 Ticks between recalculations. The trail follows the target smoothly in between, and a new navigation path from the server is applied immediately. max_path_length 32.0 Longest path shown, measured along the path itself from the target. track ["players", "hostile", "neutral", "projectiles"] What is shown. One list that mixes categories with specific entity types and tags. See below. ignore [] Anything matching here is never shown, even if it matches track. Same entries as track.

docs.title: What track and ignore take
docs.text:
Both are a single list. Each entry is one of:

Entry Matches players Other players. hostile Anything implementing Enemy. neutral Anything implementing NeutralMob. passive Any other mob. projectiles Any Projectile entity, including modded ones. mobs hostile, neutral and passive together. all Every category above. namespace:entity One entity type, such as minecraft:villager. It matches whatever its category is, so it works for things outside the categories, like armor stands. #namespace:tag An entity type tag, such as #minecraft:skeletons.

So ["hostile", "projectiles"] tracks every hostile mob and every projectile, ["mobs", "players"] tracks all mobs and players, and ["all"] with "ignore": ["minecraft:armor_stand"] tracks everything except armor stands. An entry that is not one of these stops the power from loading, and the error names the entry.

Entity paths

Property Default Meaning show_entity_paths true Paths for mobs and players. predict_entity_movement true Prediction for entities that have no navigation path. entity_prediction_time 2.0 Seconds ahead that movement is predicted.

Projectile paths

Property Default Meaning show_projectile_paths true Flight paths of projectiles. projectile_prediction_time 3.0 Seconds ahead that flight is simulated. show_projectile_impact true A particle at the predicted impact point. show_time_to_impact false The time left before impact, such as 0.8s, written above the impact point. impact_particle minecraft:end_rod The particle used as the marker. preview_aimed_shots false Instead of following projectiles after they are fired, show the path a shot would take for as long as its shooter is aiming. See below. aim_charge_color #FFD23F Only for preview_aimed_shots. The colour of the line when the shot has just started being drawn; it shifts to the projectile trail's own colour as the draw builds, so the trail colour means ready. See below.

Trails and rendering

Property Default Meaning entity_trail argon:path_vision_entity The Palladium trail that draws entity paths. projectile_trail argon:path_vision_projectile The Palladium trail that draws projectile paths. trail_render_distance 64.0 Paths of targets farther than this from the camera are not drawn. trail_smoothing 0.7 How much navigation corners are rounded, from 0 (the raw route) to 1 (the smoothest). A rounded stretch that would pass through a block is left sharp instead, so corners around walls stay corners. render_through_walls false Draw the trail through blocks.

docs.title: Where paths come from
docs.text:
A target gets its path from the first of these that applies, and nothing is drawn if none does.

  1. Actual AI navigation. The server reads the mob's own navigation path and sends the nodes that are still ahead of it. It reads the path the mob already has: it never asks Minecraft to compute a new route, so it cannot change what the mob does. The trail follows the real nodes, so a route around a wall is drawn as the route around the wall. Only mobs with a path that is in progress show one, and the server sends nothing for the rest.
  2. Predicted movement, for anything else that is moving: players, entities with custom movement, and mobs that are moving without a navigation path. The client takes the entity's recent velocity (smoothed over a few ticks) and walks it forward for entity_prediction_time: horizontal speed is kept, gravity and drag apply to anything that is falling, walls stop the path, and flying entities keep a straight line. This is an estimate of where the entity goes if it carries on, not a known destination, so the further ahead it looks the less it can be trusted. An entity that is standing still gets no path.
  3. Projectiles are simulated with Minecraft's own per-tick rules, from the projectile's current position and velocity.

docs.title: Projectile prediction
docs.text:
The physics are chosen from the kind of projectile, using the gravity the entity itself reports:

Projectile Order each tick Arrows and tridents Water drag (0.6, tridents 0.99), move, air drag 0.99, then gravity. Thrown items (snowballs, eggs, ender pearls, potions) Gravity, then drag (0.99 in air, 0.8 in water), then move. Fireballs Acceleration along the movement, then drag (0.95 in air, 0.8 in water), then move. No gravity. Any other projectile The thrown item rules, as a fallback.

The simulation stops at the first of: the prediction time, max_path_length, a block hit (a block raycast each tick, so it cannot pass through a wall), an entity hit (checked against the other targets and the holder, not the projectile's owner), or the edge of the loaded world. The path ends at the hit point and the impact marker and time are only shown when a hit was found. A projectile that is not moving, such as an arrow stuck in a block, shows nothing.

docs.title: Previewing aimed shots
docs.text:
With "preview_aimed_shots": true, projectiles are no longer followed once they are in flight. Instead, anything that is aiming a ranged weapon shows the path its shot would take, and the path stays up for as long as it keeps aiming and goes when it stops. It uses the projectile_trail, the same impact marker and the same time to impact, and it follows the same track and ignore lists as everything else, so the shooters are whoever you track.

Weapon When a path is shown Shot speed Bow While it is being drawn, once the arrow would fire (a player's draw power sets the speed). Players: draw power times 3. Mobs: 1.6. Trident While it is held ready, after the 10 tick draw for players. Players 2.5, mobs 1.6. Crossbow While it is loaded. Players 3.15, mobs 1.6. Fireworks are not predicted.

The line also shows how close the shot is to being fired. It starts as aim_charge_color and blends into the projectile trail's own colour as the bow is drawn, a player's draw power or a skeleton's 20 tick draw, so the trail's colour means the shot is ready. A loaded crossbow and a trident are always ready. Set aim_charge_color to the trail's colour to turn this off. The blend changes the colour of the trail's lines and ribbons (gradient and lightning trails), not copies drawn by an after image trail.

A player's path uses their real aim and their own movement, like the arrow would. A mob's path uses the direction it is looking and, if that lines up with a tracked entity (including you), the same upward correction vanilla gives a mob's aim at its target, so a skeleton aiming at you shows the arc that would actually reach you. The path ends at the first block or tracked entity it would hit, and a shot that would hit you shows the impact and the time left. A loaded crossbow counts as aiming, so a player standing with one loaded keeps a path up.

A shot is never exactly the line. Vanilla adds a little random spread to every shot, about one degree for a player's bow and several degrees for a skeleton depending on difficulty, and the line shows the middle of it. Everything else is taken from the same rules the game uses: where the arrow spawns (a tenth of a block below the eyes), its speed, drag, gravity, and the first block or living entity it would hit, whether or not you are tracking that entity. The line updates every tick.

The client cannot see who a mob is targeting, only what it is looking at and holding. A mob that is aiming without looking at the target yet, or an unusual mob with its own shooting rules, can show a path that does not match the real shot.

docs.title: Palladium trails
docs.text:
Path Vision reuses Palladium's own trail renderers. A trail is a normal palladium/trails/<path>.json file, and entity_trail and projectile_trail are their IDs. Palladium's trail system draws a trail behind a moving entity from recorded history, so Argon builds the trail segments from the predicted path instead and hands them to the same renderer. Argon's two defaults are gradient trails in assets/argon/palladium/trails/:

{
    "requires_movement": false,
    "renderer": {
        "type": "palladium:gradient",
        "color": "#33E6FF",
        "opacity": 0.6,
        "orientation": "horizontal",
        "offset": 0.0
    }
}

To use another look, make your own trail file in the same place and name it in the power. Use horizontal for a ribbon lying along the path and vertical for a wall of the target's height.

The appearance is all in the trail file, not in the ability, so a power only names which trail to use. What is read from it:

  • renderer: the type and all of its own settings, such as colour, opacity, orientation and the lightning settings. This is where the opacity of a path is set.
  • lifetime: the ticks a path takes to fade in when a target appears and to fade out when it leaves the radius or stops having a path. 0 is instant. If a trail file holds several trails, the longest lifetime is used.
  • offset: moves every point of the path, in blocks.
  • spacing: for after image trails, the gap between copies. See below.

What is not used, because a path has no history to space or age: tick_delay, requires_movement and anchor. The far end of a path also fades a little, and the width of an entity path is the target's own width, while projectile paths (in flight or aimed) are a thin line, 0.08 of a block wide.

Renderer Works along a path palladium:gradient Yes. palladium:lightning Yes. palladium:after_image Yes, as spaced copies of the target. See below. palladium:lightning_aura No. It is drawn around an entity's model parts, so it is skipped.

Ribbon trails are lifted a few centimetres off the ground (a little more with distance from the camera) so they do not flicker against the block surface they lie on.

docs.title: Ghost trail
docs.text:
argon:path_vision_ghost draws the target as faded copies of itself walking ahead along its path, using palladium:after_image:

{
    "spacing": 2.5,
    "lifetime": 5,
    "requires_movement": false,
    "renderer": {
        "type": "palladium:after_image",
        "color": "#FFFFFF",
        "opacity": 0.22
    }
}

Use it with "entity_trail": "argon:path_vision_ghost". For after image trails the trail's spacing is used, as a multiple of the target's width, to place the copies along the path (at least half a block apart), and at most ten copies are drawn per target, the nearest ones, and at most 24 across all targets together, because every copy is a full draw of the model. Each copy faces the direction the path is heading and gets its own walking phase from how far along the path it is, so the copies read as a stride. A copy keeps the look the target had when the copy was first created, such as its armour and held items. A lower opacity is more ghostly; color tints the copies and white leaves them untinted. Copy this file into your own pack and change those two values for a different ghost.

render_through_walls swaps Palladium's laser render types (gradient and lightning) for versions that ignore depth, only for Path Vision's own trails. Nothing else in the game is changed.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text:
Nothing is shown to anyone but the player who is using the ability. It is drawn only on that player's own client, and only while that ability is enabled: another player who has Path Vision but has it off sees nothing, and sees nothing of the holder's paths either. If the ability stops being ticked, for example on leaving a world, the client switches it off by itself after three ticks. If a power has two Path Vision abilities, only the one that switched it on can switch it off.

The server only sends path data to a player whose Path Vision is enabled right now. The server picks the targets from the ability's own detection_radius, filters and max_targets, so a client cannot ask for anything. It sends navigation nodes (not world data), only when a path actually changes, quantised to 1/16 of a block, and lists targets whose path ended so the client drops them. Everything else, including projectile and movement prediction, is calculated on the client from positions and velocities the client already has. No packets are sent every frame.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Predictions are estimates. Another player can turn at any moment and a mob can change its mind; the path updates as soon as it does, but it can never show what has not been decided.
  • Movement prediction follows the centre line of the body, so it can stop early at a one block step that the entity would jump.
  • Impact tests use block collision and the bounding boxes of the other targets; an entity that is not a current target is not hit, and entity hit boxes are widened a little for the projectile's size.
  • Projectiles with custom flight that Argon cannot read are drawn with the fallback rules and may be wrong. Leave them out with ignore.
  • Mobs that use their own movement controller instead of Minecraft navigation show a prediction, not a route.

docs.title: argon:throwable_item
docs.text: One reusable Palladium ability that makes any item throwable. The projectile looks like the real item, keeps the exact item with all its data, can bounce or embed in blocks, damage and embed in entities, return on its own, be recalled, hit enemies on the way back, home in, ricochet, be steered through a camera, and be caught. Everything is configured in the ability JSON; nothing is specific to one item.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Everything except item is optional, and so is every section and every key inside a section.

{
  "type": "argon:throwable_item",
  "item": "fsang:mjolnir",
  "hand": "main_hand",
  "throw":        { "speed": 2.6, "windup": 5, "gravity_mode": "none", "drag": 1.0, "maximum_time": 160 },
  "combat":       { "damage": 9, "maximum_targets": 3, "entity_impact": "continue" },
  "block_impact": { "mode": "embed" },
  "return":       { "triggers": ["after_hit"], "speed": 3.0, "block_collision": "pass_through", "damage_enabled": true, "recall": true },
  "targeting":    { "mode": "none" },
  "homing":       { "accuracy": 100 },
  "ricochet":     { "enabled": false },
  "steering":     { "mode": "none" },
  "camera":       { "distance": 5 },
  "perfect_catch": { "enabled": true },
  "pin":          { "enabled": true, "duration": 0 },
  "deflection":   { "enabled": false },
  "render":       { "scale": 1.8, "rotation_mode": "spin", "rotation_axis": "x", "rotation_offset": [180, 0, 0] },
  "sounds":       { "throw": "fsang:mjolnir_throw", "flight": "fsang:mjolnir_flight" },
  "state": { "enabling": { "type": "palladium:key_bind", "behaviour": "activation", "time": 11, "cooldown": 10 } }
}

Every number that is a Value can be driven by Palladium (power age, data attachments, molang) and is read when the item is thrown, except the return settings (speed, acceleration, turn_rate, accuracy, maximum_duration, damage_multiplier, catch_radius), which are read again at the moment of recall.

docs.title: Sections and keys
docs.text:
• item / hand / pickup: item (id, list or tag; required), hand (main_hand, off_hand, either), pickup.on_touch (true) and pickup.radius (1.5): the owner picks the item up by walking near it while it is embedded in a block or resting.
  • throw: speed (1.8), windup (0 ticks; the item stays in the hand and the aim is taken at release), gravity_mode (none, vanilla, scaled), gravity (1), drag (0.99), inaccuracy (0), inherit_owner_velocity (0.35), maximum_time (200), maximum_distance (96), maximum_owner_distance (128), out_of_range (return, recover or drop; the item is never deleted).
  • combat: damage (6), knockback (0.6), damage_type, maximum_targets (1, 0 = unlimited), entity_impact (continue, bounce, return, stop, embed), allow_repeat_targets, rehit_cooldown (10).
  • block_impact: mode (bounce, embed, return, drop, stop), restitution (0.6), friction (0.85), maximum_bounces (3), embed_depth (0.3), embed_duration (0 = until recalled or picked up).
  • return: triggers (a list of none, after_hit, after_block_impact, after_timeout, after_distance, always), timeout (60), distance (32), speed (2.4), acceleration (0.3), turn_rate (30), accuracy (100), maximum_duration (200), block_collision (pass_through, stop), damage_enabled, damage_multiplier, maximum_damage_targets, catch_radius (1.25), recall.
  • targeting: mode (none, automatic, marked, hybrid), accuracy (100), detection_range (16), cone (90), line_of_sight (true), filter (hostile, living, players, non_players), entity_types, priority (nearest, look_direction, lowest_health, random).
  • homing: accuracy (100), turn_rate (14), acceleration, max_speed, prediction, target_offset (0.5), lost_target (continue, reacquire, return).
  • ricochet: enabled, maximum, target_range (10), speed (2.6), turn_rate (40), damage_multiplier.
  • steering: mode (none, look_direction, projectile_camera), turn_rate (10), strength (1), maximum_speed (0 = the throw speed), acceleration (0.08), return_on_release, owner_control (normal, limited, immobile).
  • camera: distance (5), fov (0 = unchanged), smoothing (0.35), roll (0).
  • perfect_catch: enabled, window (8), damage_bonus (1.5), bonus_duration (100).
  • pin: enabled, duration (60; 0 = until recalled), distance (4).
  • deflection: enabled, radius (1.6), strength (1), target_filter.
  • render: scale (1 = the item model at its full block size; flat item sprites like swords are a block across, so 0.6 to 0.8 usually looks right), rotation_mode (none, spin, tumble), rotation_speed (36), rotation_axis (x, y, z), rotation_offset ([x, y, z] degrees), face_velocity (true), embed_spin_angle.
  • sounds: plain sound ids from sounds.json, all optional: throw, entity_hit, block_hit, recall, return, catch, flight (loops while flying).

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
1. Pressing the key (a palladium:key_bind with behaviour: activation) while the item is in the chosen hand throws it. The item leaves the hand and is saved in a per-player record (full ItemStack, original slot, projectile id) in the argon:thrown_records attachment. No placeholder is left, so there is no second copy.
  2. Pressing the same key while the item is out recalls it (needs return.recall).
  3. The projectile is server-driven; the client only interpolates and renders.
  4. The item returns to its original slot (or any free slot, or the owner's feet if full) when it is caught, picked up, recovered by a safety rule, or when the owner logs out, dies, changes dimension or logs back in. The record is removed before the item is given back, so it is restored exactly once, and a watchdog restores it if the projectile disappears.
  5. Phases: OUTBOUND (swept in sub-steps of at most 0.9 blocks), EMBEDDED in a block, EMBEDDED in an entity, RESTING, RETURNING (turns toward the owner's chest at return.turn_rate times return.accuracy, caught inside catch_radius; return.maximum_duration restores the item directly as a safety net).

docs.title: Targeting, homing and ricochet
docs.text:
• targeting.mode: none (no selection; ricochet still picks its own targets), automatic, marked (only targets marked with argon:throw_marker, in the order marked) or hybrid (marked first, then automatic).
  • Acquisition attempts happen at the throw, after each ricochet and when a target is lost. Each succeeds with targeting.accuracy percent when the mode is automatic or hybrid, rolled on the server. It is never re-rolled every tick, never stops a real collision from hitting, and marked targets need no roll.
  • Candidates must be inside detection_range (and, for the first target, the cone), visible when line_of_sight is on, pass filter and entity_types, and not be the owner, allies, the owner's pets, or players the owner may not harm.
  • Homing is separate from acquisition: homing.accuracy scales homing.turn_rate. Accuracy 0 acquires a target but never steers. A target that dies, leaves range or stays out of sight for more than 12 ticks follows homing.lost_target. Gravity and drag are skipped while chasing.
  • Ricochet flies on to the next valid target after each hit (physically, at ricochet.speed and ricochet.turn_rate, damage times damage_multiplier), up to ricochet.maximum (0 = one fewer than combat.maximum_targets), then the return rules apply. Targets already struck are skipped unless allow_repeat_targets.
  • argon:throw_marker marks (or unmarks) the living entity you look at, up to maximum_marked_targets. Marks are shown only to the marker as sparks, cleared on logout, and used up by the next marked or hybrid throw.

docs.title: Steering and the projectile camera
docs.text:
• Set steering.mode to look_direction or projectile_camera and give the player an argon:throw_steer ability with a held key bind. While held, every flying projectile of theirs with a mode turns toward where they look. Gravity, drag and homing are off while steering. Letting go hands the projectile back to its normal flight, or sends it back with return_on_release.
  • projectile_camera also moves the camera to a chase view behind the projectile (camera.distance, clipped by blocks) with optional fov, smoothing and roll. The player stays the camera entity, so movement, look and packets keep working. Argon's flight and gravity camera adjustments, the wall-crawl roll, the first-person hand and first-person screen overlays are skipped while it is active.
  • The camera ends the moment the key is released, the projectile hits something that stops it, is recalled, caught or removed, or the owner dies, logs out or changes dimension; the client also drops it by itself if the projectile entity disappears.
  • owner_control while the camera is active: normal, limited (movement speed -65 percent) or immobile (no walking or jumping), done with transient attribute modifiers.

docs.title: Pinning, deflection, perfect catch and animations
docs.text:
• pin: a mob hit by the outbound item is moved against a wall within pin.distance behind it and held there (maximum slowness, position locked) for pin.duration ticks, or with 0 until the owner recalls (refreshed every second so a crash cannot leave anything slowed). While a mob is pinned the item does not start an automatic return at all; it stops and falls where it is. Players, the Ender Dragon, the Wither and #c:bosses are never pinned.
  • entity_impact: embed: the item lodges in the mob it hits and follows it until recalled, the mob dies (it then falls) or block_impact.embed_duration runs out. Ends the throw at that hit; does not combine with ricochet.
  • deflection: while flying, any projectile within radius that is not the owner's is reversed with vanilla's deflection and becomes the owner's.
  • perfect_catch: pressing the ability while the item is returning and within window ticks of arriving catches it at once; the next throw within bonus_duration ticks deals damage_bonus times damage.
  • argon:throw_event is a condition that is true for a number of ticks after the entity threw, recalled or caught with a throwable (event, ticks, optional arm right or left to match the player's main arm), so animation controllers can play throw, recall and catch clips and mirrored ones for left-handed players. The times are a synced attachment, so other players see them too.

docs.title: Damage
docs.text: Damage uses combat.damage_type if set, otherwise the vanilla thrown-projectile source attributed to the owner. The item's own attack damage and enchantments are not added, so nothing is applied twice. The owner, allies, the owner's tamed pets, spectators and players the owner may not harm are skipped.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Removing the power while the item is out does not interrupt the flight; the item still returns, can be picked up, or is restored on logout, death or dimension change.
  • The release point is computed from the shoulder and the look direction, not read from the player model, so it can sit slightly off the visible hand with some animations and suits.

docs.title: Wall Crawling with directional gravity
docs.text: argon:wall_crawling lets a player climb walls and cross ceilings. It has two modes. With "use_directional_gravity": true it works on directional gravity: the surface the player is on becomes their floor, so the hitbox, eyes, camera, model, jumping and fall damage all follow. With it off (the default) the player is steered along the surface by the original crawl. The two never run at once for the same ability.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
• Attaching. Walking into a wall from the ground turns you up it. In the air, a wall (or a ceiling, if allowed) within surface_detection_range is grabbed. Slabs, stairs and other steps you could just walk up do not count as walls.
  • Surfaces are real collision. Every question the crawl asks is a sweep of the actual hitbox against the blocks' collision shapes, so slabs, fences, trapdoors, walls and modded blocks are what they really are, and a surface only counts if it is under the body.
  • Corners. The directions you are heading toward are tried best-aligned first; for each, an obstacle ahead taller than a step turns you onto it (inside corner, wall to ceiling, ceiling to wall, wall to floor), and the connected surface running out under your next step turns you round the edge (outside corner, wall to roof, wall to wall). Both pivot about the edge, so you stay in contact with the surface you left, and a turn is moved by the smallest nudge needed to clear a block it grazes. There is no fixed cooldown: what stops two nearby surfaces flickering is that turning straight back to the surface you just left is refused for 12 ticks unless you have clearly started moving back.
  • Roofs. After climbing onto a roof you keep crawling on it (steered by the same heading) so you can walk across and back down over any edge. It ends when you jump, leave the ground, or stop moving for two seconds.
  • Controls. In surface_relative mode W goes along a heading kept on the surface, not toward the camera: up a wall, or the way you faced across a floor or ceiling. The heading is carried round every corner, so looking around never changes where W goes. In camera_relative mode the heading is the camera direction flattened onto the surface; movement is tangent to the surface either way.
  • Speed. base_speed times speed_multiplier times surface_speed_multiplier, along the surface only; sprinting multiplies by 1.3 if allowed. Gravity into the surface is separate and gravity_strength scales it.
  • Jumping. Pushes you straight off the surface by surface_jump_strength, keeping your speed along it, and the surface cannot be grabbed again for 8 ticks. Detaching from height falls and takes fall damage normally; staying attached never accumulates fall distance.
  • Tight spaces. If the full-height body does not fit on the next surface but the crawl-sized one does, and auto_crawl is on, you turn onto it crawl-sized (vanilla's pose logic does the rest).
  • Surface disappears. If the surface under you is gone for 2 ticks you move onto the nearest other surface, or let go and fall.
  • Other abilities. The crawl lets go whenever something else needs the player's movement: Palladium flight, creative flight, a Charged Takeoff, a web swing in hand, gliding, swimming, a vehicle, spectator, death, or the ability ending. The crawl never fights them for the velocity.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text: The client chooses the surface (as it does for ordinary movement), turns gravity at once, and tells the server, which checks there is a surface at the reported position and makes it official; other players then see the turn. A choice the server refuses is answered with the server's gravity, which the client adopts. The server also drops the crawl if there has been no surface near the body for about two seconds. Only changes are sent.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
These properties belong to the directional gravity mode. Where one is not set it falls back to the matching original property, written in the Default column:

Property Default Notes use_directional_gravity false Turns everything below on. gravity_strength 1.0 Multiplier on gravity while attached. rotate_camera camera_roll Whether the camera turns with the surface. false keeps the view upright to the world. camera_transition_time 6 Ticks for the camera to turn. 0 is instant. smooth_transitions true false makes every turn instant. transition_duration 6 Ticks for the drawn body to turn. transition_easing ease_in_out linear, ease_in, ease_out, ease_in_out. surface_detection_range attach_distance (0.5) How close a surface must be to grab or keep. surface_transition_tolerance 0.15 How far before an edge the turn starts, 0 to 0.3. movement_mode surface_relative Or camera_relative. surface_jump_strength detach_strength Push off the surface when jumping. auto_crawl true Allow turning onto surfaces only a crawl-sized body fits. allow_ceiling_crawling ceiling_crawling Ceilings are valid surfaces. allow_corner_transitions true Turn at corners and from floor onto a wall. false leaves only grabbing from the air. preserve_surface_momentum true Keep speed through a turn. surface_speed_multiplier 1.0 Extra multiplier on speed along the surface. allow_surface_sprinting true play_running_animation true Sprinting along a wall or ceiling plays the running animation (legs and arms swinging). Vanilla only starts it from how far you move across the ground, which is nothing while climbing. Only while sprinting. crawl_when_not_sprinting false On a wall or ceiling the player is crawl-sized (vanilla crawling pose, a 0.6 block hitbox that fits one-block gaps) unless sprinting. Sprinting stands them back up as far as there is room. The server applies the same rule, so both use the same hitbox. view_orientation relative relative: a turn keeps the same look angles in the new gravity. world: it keeps the same point in the world.

In this mode third_person_camera_roll and gravity_pull_strength do nothing; the whole camera turns in either perspective, and gravity does the pulling.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Spider-Man style, using the original speeds:

{
    "type": "argon:wall_crawling",
    "use_directional_gravity": true,
    "ceiling_crawling": true,
    "base_speed": 0.5,
    "speed_multiplier": 0.75,
    "detach_strength": 1.0,
    "rotate_camera": true,
    "movement_mode": "surface_relative",
    "auto_crawl": true
}

A slower climber that keeps the camera upright and stays off ceilings:

{
    "type": "argon:wall_crawling",
    "use_directional_gravity": true,
    "base_speed": 0.1,
    "rotate_camera": false,
    "allow_ceiling_crawling": false,
    "allow_corner_transitions": false,
    "surface_speed_multiplier": 0.5,
    "allow_surface_sprinting": false
}

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Looking straight into the surface you stand on is a gimbal point of any yaw-and-pitch camera: a tiny change of aim there can swing the roll. A turn itself does not spin the view, but aiming straight at your feet while on a wall can roll the view as you move the mouse.
  • Flight, a takeoff, a web swing and gliding make the crawl let go; it does not resume by itself until the player lands or lets go of them and touches a surface again.
  • Swimming and lava let go too; there is no crawling in water.
  • The player's own Takeoff, web and appendage animations are not aware of being on a wall.
  • Climbing an unbroken wall relies on the wall being under the whole body footprint; a wall of a single thin block, or one broken by gaps wider than the tolerance, is crossed by turning round it.

docs.title: Tech Table
docs.text:
The Tech Table (argon:tech_table) is a workbench for powered gear. It has three tabs, and a pack sets all of them up with JSON.

Tab What the player does Where a pack defines it Craft Runs timed recipes on a 5x5 grid. data/<namespace>/recipe/ Modify Installs modules on a suit or a device. data/<namespace>/argon/suit_modification/ Customize Puts items into an item's own slots, presses its buttons and picks its colors. data/<namespace>/argon/tech_table_customization/

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
• Use a module for an upgrade that costs materials, can have levels, and can be permanent. See Modules.
  • Use a Customize slot for a part the player can swap in and out freely, such as a casing, a chip or a core. See Customize Slots.

Both can use the same module functions to change an item, give it a power or add stats.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
data/<namespace>/recipe/<name>.json, "type": "argon:tech_table_crafting".

{
  "type": "argon:tech_table_crafting",
  "pattern": ["ccc", "cdc", "ccc"],
  "key": { "c": "minecraft:copper_ingot", "d": { "ingredient": "minecraft:diamond", "count": 2 } },
  "tool": { "ingredient": "minecraft:shears", "mode": "damaged", "amount": 3 },
  "result": { "item": { "id": "minecraft:diamond", "count": 2 } },
  "name": { "translate": "recipe.mypack.diamonds" },
  "time": 200
}
Key Description Required Fallback pattern and key A shaped recipe of any size up to 5x5. One of pattern or ingredients None ingredients A shapeless recipe with up to 25 entries. One of pattern or ingredients None mirror Whether a shaped recipe also works mirrored. No true tool An item that has to be in the separate tool slot. mode is consumed, retained or damaged, with amount for damage. No None (mode: retained) result {"item": ...}, or {"suit_set": "namespace:path"} to give every piece of a Palladium suit set. Yes name The name shown above the preview. No None time Crafting time in ticks. 0 is instant. No 100

When the player presses Craft, the table takes the ingredients and runs a timer. It keeps going with the screen closed, and the finished items wait in the output slots.

docs.title: Customize Slots
docs.text:
A customization file gives an item its own slots, buttons and color pickers on the Tech Table's Customize tab. The player puts the item in the top slot, and everything the pack defined for it appears.

data/<namespace>/argon/tech_table_customization/<name>.json

docs.title: A full example
docs.text:
A gauntlet that takes a core and a dye chip.

{
  "items": "example:gauntlet",
  "slots": [
    {
      "id": "example:core",
      "accepts": "#example:gauntlet_cores",
      "preview": "minecraft:diamond",
      "functions": [
        { "type": "argon:add_power", "power": "example:gauntlet_powered", "slots": "mainhand" }
      ],
      "variants": [
        {
          "items": "minecraft:netherite_ingot",
          "functions": [
            { "type": "argon:attribute_modifier", "attribute": "minecraft:attack_damage", "amount": 4, "slots": "mainhand" },
            { "type": "argon:tooltip", "text": "Netherite core" }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "example:dye_chip",
      "accepts": "example:chip"
    }
  ],
  "toggles": [
    {
      "id": "example:overdrive",
      "title": "Overdrive",
      "requires": ["example:core"],
      "functions": [ { "type": "argon:tooltip", "text": "Overdrive on" } ]
    }
  ],
  "colors": [
    {
      "id": "example:trim",
      "title": "Trim",
      "component": "minecraft:dyed_color",
      "requires": ["example:dye_chip"]
    }
  ]
}

While a core is in the gauntlet, it gives the power in the main hand. A netherite core also adds attack damage. The Overdrive button appears once a core is in, and the Trim color picker appears once the chip is in.

docs.title: File settings
docs.text: Key Description Required Fallback items The item, item tag ("#namespace:tag") or list of them that the file applies to. Yes slots The item's slots. No Empty toggles The item's buttons. No Empty colors The item's color pickers. No Empty replace true throws away what earlier files defined for the item. No false priority Files with a higher number are applied later. No 0

docs.title: Slots
docs.text: Key Description Required Fallback id A unique name for the slot. The inserted item is saved under it. Yes accepts Items or item tags that can go in. Yes preview An item shown faintly while the slot is empty. No None max_stack How many items fit, from 1 to 99. No 1 functions Module functions active while the slot is filled. No Empty variants Extra functions for particular inserted items. Each has items and functions. No Empty legacy_index Reads an item saved in the vanilla container component at this position, for items that used the older Java slot system. No None

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text: Key Description Required Fallback id A unique name for the button. Yes title The button's label. Yes on Text shown after the title while on. No "ON" off Text shown after the title while off. No "OFF" component A true or false data component to store the state in, so models and render layers can read it. No Stored by Argon requires Slot IDs that must be filled for the button to appear. No Empty functions Functions active while the button is on. No Empty off_functions Functions active while the button is off. No Empty

docs.title: Color pickers
docs.text:
Key Description Required Fallback id A unique name for the picker. Yes title The name shown above the sliders when there are several pickers. Yes component The data component the color is written to. It has to accept a number, or be minecraft:dyed_color. Yes requires Slot IDs that must be filled for the picker to appear. Emptying one removes the color. No Empty

The player picks a color with the red, green and blue sliders or types a hex code.

docs.title: Functions that work here
docs.text: Customize files can use argon:set_component, argon:copy_component, argon:item_id_to_component, argon:add_power, argon:attribute_modifier and argon:tooltip. The capacity, number and custom value effects only work on modules, and a file that uses one in a slot is rejected with an error in the log.

docs.title: Reading slots in a power
docs.text:
Powers added by argon:add_power need nothing else. For your own powers, two conditions check an item's slots and buttons:

"state": {
  "enabling": {
    "type": "argon:has_tech_slot_item",
    "slot": "mainhand",
    "tech_slot": "example:core",
    "items": "minecraft:netherite_ingot"
  }
}

"state": { "enabling": { "type": "argon:tech_toggle", "slot": "mainhand", "toggle": "example:overdrive" } }

See Conditions for every setting.

docs.title: Several files for one item
docs.text:
Files that match the same item are merged, so an add-on can give another pack's item a new slot without copying its file.

  • Files are applied in order of priority, then by file name.
  • A slot, button or color picker with the same id as an earlier one replaces it.
  • replace: true discards everything applied before that file.

The tab shows three slots and three buttons at a time. With more than that, arrows appear, and the mouse wheel scrolls the slot column.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Customization files reload with /reload. An item that already has parts in it picks up a changed file the next time something on it is changed at a Tech Table.
  • Inserted items are saved on the base item, so they travel with it.
  • When a function stops applying, the components it set go back to the item's default. Attribute bonuses from other sources are left alone.
  • Do not let two sources manage the same component on one item, because the one worked out last wins.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
A module is an upgrade the player installs on the Modify tab, either on a full Palladium suit or on a single device item.

data/<namespace>/argon/suit_modification/<name>.json

{
  "category": "passive",
  "suits": ["example:runner_suit"],
  "icon": { "item": "minecraft:feather" },
  "requirements": [ { "ingredient": "minecraft:feather", "count": 4 } ],
  "max_level": 3,
  "removal": "removable",
  "effects": [
    { "type": "argon:attribute_modifier", "attribute": "minecraft:movement_speed", "amount": 0.1, "operation": "add_multiplied_base", "pieces": ["feet"] },
    { "type": "argon:tooltip", "text": "Light soles fitted", "pieces": ["feet"] }
  ]
}

docs.title: Settings

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
A module's effects change the item it is installed on. They are worked out again whenever something is installed or removed, so taking everything off puts the item back the way it was.

Every type is listed with its settings on the Module Functions page.

docs.title: On a suit
docs.text:
A suit has several pieces, so each function chooses where it goes:

  • Powers and attribute bonuses go on the chestplate, or on the first piece the suit has.
  • The other functions go on every piece.
  • Set pieces to choose, for example ["head", "chest"].

The capacity, number and custom value effects apply to every piece.

docs.title: A value that depends on the material
docs.text:
Say a module accepts three different cores, and a number should depend on which one was used:

"requirements": [ { "ingredient": ["minecraft:redstone_block", "minecraft:diamond_block", "minecraft:netherite_ingot"], "count": 1 } ],
"max_level": 3,
"effects": [ {
  "type": "argon:custom_value",
  "key": "example:core_power",
  "values": [
    { "item": "minecraft:redstone_block", "value": 2 },
    { "item": "minecraft:diamond_block", "value": 5 },
    { "item": "minecraft:netherite_ingot", "value": 10 }
  ],
  "fallback": 1,
  "tooltip": "Core Power: %s"
} ]

Each level adds its own number (so 2 + 5 + 10 = 17), and removing a level takes the last one off. A power reads it with the argon:item_custom_value value (slot, key, fallback), for example as a beam's max_distance.

docs.title: Checking for a module in a power
docs.text:
argon:has_suit_modification is true while a module is installed on the worn suit. It takes modification, and optionally suit, slot (to check a device instead) and min_level.

"state": { "enabling": { "type": "argon:has_suit_modification", "modification": "example:reserve_battery" } }

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Modules are saved on the items, not on the player, so they go wherever the item goes. A suit only counts as having a module while every piece has it.
  • Module files are loaded from the normal data pack folders, not Palladium's addon loader. Rejoin the world after changing them.
